lessons.title: Understand a website
lessons.concept: Explain the difference between a browser and a server.

explanation.text: Your browser displays the site. A server receives requests and sends responses. A database keeps information that must last, such as products and orders.
Imagine a shop: the window is what the customer sees; staff check their request; a ledger keeps the orders.

annotations.label: fetch sends a request to this address.
Check the status before reading the data.
json reads the structured response data.

exercise.task:
Complete the function name that requests products from the server.
const response = await ____("/api/products");
hints: Read the first example line: the name comes just after await.
exercise.solution:
const response = await fetch("/api/products");

fetch sends the request. await waits for the response before continuing.

quiz.question: What displays the page for the customer?
quiz.explanation: The browser displays the interface. The server handles requests; the database stores data.
answerExplanations: The browser reads the response and displays the page to the customer.
GitHub stores code and its history. The browser displays the page.
The database stores data. The browser displays the page.

summary: Frontend: the visible interface. Backend: processing on the server.
lessons.why: Imagine a shop: the window is what the customer sees; staff check their request; a ledger keeps the orders.
lessons.whatIf: The screen should explain what happens: waiting, a response, or an error. An error does not mean the request succeeded.

teaching.what: Explain the difference between a browser and a server.
teaching.why: Imagine a shop: the window is what the customer sees; staff check their request; a ledger keeps the orders.
teaching.how:
fetch sends a request to this address.
Check the status before reading the data.
json reads the structured response data.
teaching.breaks: The screen should explain what happens: waiting, a response, or an error. An error does not mean the request succeeded.
teaching.modify:
Complete the function name that requests products from the server.
const response = await ____("/api/products");

lessons.title: Write what people see
lessons.concept: Recognize a heading and a paragraph in code.

explanation.text: HTML gives content a structure. An h1 heading introduces the main subject; a p paragraph contains text. React uses similar syntax called JSX.
Like a document: headings, paragraphs and sections each have a role.

annotations.label: h1 opens the heading; /h1 closes it.
p opens a text paragraph.

exercise.task:
Close the heading with the same tag it starts with. Write only its name.
<h1>My shop</____>
hints: The opening tag is <h1>. The slash / marks the closing tag.
exercise.solution:
My shop

starts the main heading;

ends it.

quiz.question: Which tag represents the main heading?
quiz.explanation: h1 describes the main heading. p describes a paragraph and button an action.
answerExplanations: p represents a paragraph. h1 represents the main heading.
h1 identifies the main heading: it gives meaning to the content.
button represents a clickable action. h1 represents the main heading.

summary: A way to write an interface in a JavaScript or TypeScript file.
lessons.why: Like a document: headings, paragraphs and sections each have a role.
lessons.whatIf: The text changes, but it is still a heading. Tags surround the content.

teaching.what: Recognize a heading and a paragraph in code.
teaching.why: Like a document: headings, paragraphs and sections each have a role.
teaching.how:
h1 opens the heading; /h1 closes it.
p opens a text paragraph.
teaching.breaks: The text changes, but it is still a heading. Tags surround the content.

lessons.title: Add visual style

explanation.text: CSS controls colors, spacing and sizes. The same content can have different appearances. This project also uses Tailwind classes to apply styles.
HTML is the shop structure; CSS is its decoration and the space between its shelves.

annotations.label: This rule targets elements with the card class.
background chooses the background color.
padding adds space inside.

quiz.explanation: padding changes presentation, not product data.
answerExplanations: padding controls inside spacing. It does not change the price.
The data stays the same. padding changes only inside spacing.
Yes: padding moves content away from the card’s inside edge.

summary: A layout that adapts to screen width.

lessons.title: Make a calculation
lessons.concept: Understand a variable and a simple calculation.

explanation.text: JavaScript lets a program calculate and react. A variable names a value. Here, the total is the price multiplied by the quantity.
A variable is a labeled box: “price”, “quantity”, “total”.

annotations.label: price names the value 100.
quantity names the number of items.
* multiplies the two values.

hints: In JavaScript, multiplication uses an asterisk, not the letter x.

quiz.question: For 2 items at 100 MAD, what is the total?
quiz.explanation: * means multiply: 100 × 2 = 200. Quantity changes the total.
answerExplanations: 100 + 2 = 102 adds price and quantity. You need to multiply them.
100 × 2 = 200: price is multiplied by the two items in the question.
100 is the price of one item. The question has two: the total is 200.

summary: Declares a name whose value cannot be reassigned.
lessons.why: A variable is a labeled box: “price”, “quantity”, “total”.
lessons.whatIf: 100 × 3 gives 300 MAD. This is a demo calculation; a real order must recheck the price on the server.

teaching.what: Understand a variable and a simple calculation.
teaching.why: A variable is a labeled box: “price”, “quantity”, “total”.
teaching.how:
price names the value 100.
quantity names the number of items.
* multiplies the two values.
teaching.breaks: 100 × 3 gives 300 MAD. This is a demo calculation; a real order must recheck the price on the server.

lessons.title: Reuse a product card
lessons.concept: Explain what a React component is.

explanation.text: A component is a reusable piece of interface. Props are the information passed to it. The same card can display different products with different names.
Like a label template: keep the template and change the product name.

annotations.label: The component receives a text prop called name.
The braces display the value of name.
The function ends here.
Use the component with a product name.

hints: Use the name of the value received by ProductCard.

quiz.question: Why reuse a component?
options: To keep the same presentation with different data
quiz.explanation: A component avoids duplicating the same interface. Props change the data it displays.
answerExplanations: The structure stays the same and props provide each product’s data.
A component organizes the display. It does not replace database storage.
Reusing a component displays different text within the same structure.

summary: Information passed to a component by its caller.
lessons.why: Like a label template: keep the template and change the product name.
lessons.whatIf: The name is data. The component decides where that data appears.

teaching.what: Explain what a React component is.
teaching.why: Like a label template: keep the template and change the product name.
teaching.how:
The component receives a text prop called name.
The braces display the value of name.
The function ends here.
Use the component with a product name.
teaching.breaks: The name is data. The component decides where that data appears.

lessons.title: React to a click

explanation.text: State is a value React keeps between renders. Updating it with its setter lets React display the new result.
Like a counter: the button changes the stored number, then the screen shows it.

annotations.label: quantity starts at 1; setQuantity changes it.
On click, add 1 to the previous value.
React displays the current quantity.

hints: It is the second name in the square brackets, with an uppercase Q.

quiz.question: What does setQuantity do?
quiz.explanation: The setter updates component state. It does not automatically save an order to the database.
answerExplanations: Publishing needs a deployment. setQuantity changes only component state.
setQuantity deletes no product. It changes the value used by the counter.
The setter changes state, then React displays the new quantity.

summary: A React tool to remember a value and update the interface.
lessons.why: Like a counter: the button changes the stored number, then the screen shows it.
lessons.whatIf: Both results use the same quantity. We update state rather than manually editing the HTML.

teaching.why: Like a counter: the button changes the stored number, then the screen shows it.
teaching.how:
quantity starts at 1; setQuantity changes it.
On click, add 1 to the previous value.
React displays the current quantity.
teaching.breaks: Both results use the same quantity. We update state rather than manually editing the HTML.

lessons.concept: Connect an address to a Next.js file.

explanation.text: This project uses the Next.js App Router. A page.tsx file inside app creates a page. Folder names provide the address path. layout.tsx provides a shared layout.
The folder is a street; page.tsx is the door that lets you enter.

annotations.label: The comment gives the file location.
The page exports its main component.
The page displays a heading.

exercise.task:
Complete the filename that creates the /boutique page.
app/boutique/____

The boutique folder gives the address. page.tsx provides the page component.

layout.tsx provides a shared layout. A page needs its page.tsx file.
package.json describes project scripts and dependencies, not page content.

lessons.title: Request data

explanation.text: An API is an access point for programs. The browser requests products; the server checks the request and sends a response. Plan for loading and errors.
Like ordering at a counter: make a specific request and wait for a response.

annotations.label: GET handles a read request.
Return an object as JSON.
The function ends.

hints: The name is the data format written in lowercase.

quiz.question: If the server does not respond, what should appear?
options: A clear error and a way to retry
quiz.explanation: The interface should reflect the actual request result. Clear feedback helps people understand and retry.
answerExplanations: An invented success misleads the customer: report the error instead.
A clear message explains the problem; retrying allows recovery after a failure.
A random price would be false data. Explain the error and offer a retry.

summary: A structured text format for exchanging data between programs.
lessons.why: Like ordering at a counter: make a specific request and wait for a response.
lessons.whatIf: An error is a state to explain to the customer. Offer a retry without showing false success.

GET handles a read request.
Return an object as JSON.
The function ends.

lessons.title: Keep information
lessons.concept: Distinguish screen state from lasting data.

explanation.text: A database keeps information organized in tables. A row represents an item; a column represents a detail. Supabase provides this project’s PostgreSQL database. Access must follow permissions.
Like a stock ledger: each row is a product; columns hold its name, price or stock.

annotations.label: products is the example table name.
id, name and price are columns.
This row represents one product.

hints: Use the English word for the product’s price, already used in the calculations.

quiz.question: Where should a lasting order be stored?
options: In the database after server validation
quiz.explanation: The server validates the order and permissions before saving. The React counter only represents interface state.
answerExplanations: A color concerns appearance. It does not store an order.
React state can disappear when leaving the page. An order needs to be saved.
The server checks data and permissions before saving the order in the database.

summary: Rules determining which data rows a user can read or change.
lessons.why: Like a stock ledger: each row is a product; columns hold its name, price or stock.
lessons.whatIf: A value on screen is not necessarily saved to a database. Real saving needs an authorized request.

teaching.why: Like a stock ledger: each row is a product; columns hold its name, price or stock.

products is the example table name.
id, name and price are columns.
This row represents one product.

lessons.title: Publish and keep learning
lessons.concept: Explain the roles of GitHub, Vercel and tests.

explanation.text: Git keeps a change history. GitHub hosts the code repository. Vercel builds and hosts the website. Before publishing, check changes with tests and a project build.
A checked draft becomes a new edition. History helps you understand what changed.

codeExample.code:
git diff
npm.cmd test
npm.cmd run build

annotations.label: See the exact changes before committing them.
Run the project tests in the Windows terminal.
Check that the site can be built.

exercise.task:
Complete the command that checks the project build.
npm.cmd run ____
hints: The word means “construct”. This command does not publish the site.
exercise.solution:
npm.cmd run build

npm.cmd run build prepares the site and reports build errors. Publishing is a separate step.

quiz.explanation: Vercel hosts the site; GitHub hosts the repository. Continue with workshops and the Academy: forms, TypeScript, security, tests, payments and projects.
